title: What is an AWS Transit Gateway, and how does it enable a hub-and-spoke topology that replaces a mesh of VPC peerings (centralized, transitive routing between many VPCs/on-prem)?
shortTitle: AWS Transit Gateway and Hub-and-Spoke Topology

s1_definition.profdef: AWS Transit Gateway is a regional network transit hub that connects many VPCs and on-premises networks through a single, centrally-managed gateway. Each VPC or VPN or Direct Connect attaches to the Transit Gateway once, and the gateway provides transitive routing between all attachments. This replaces the full mesh of point-to-point VPC peerings — where connecting N VPCs needs roughly N-squared peerings — with a hub-and-spoke where each network has just one attachment.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has twenty buildings that all need to reach each other. Peering is like building a private bridge between every pair — with twenty buildings that is around a hundred and ninety bridges, impossible to manage. A Transit Gateway is a central transport hub, like a shared metro station: each building builds just one connection to the station, and the station routes people between any two buildings. Add a new building, and it only needs one connection to the station, not a bridge to every other building.
s1_definition.oneliner: Transit Gateway is a central hub that gives transitive routing between many VPCs and on-prem with one attachment each, replacing the unmanageable N-squared mesh of peerings.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** AWS Transit Gateway is a regional network transit hub that connects many VPCs and on-premises networks through a single, centrally-managed gateway. Each VPC or VPN or Direct Connect attaches to the Transit Gateway once, and the gateway provides transitive routing between all attachments. This replaces the full mesh of point-to-point VPC peerings — where connecting N VPCs needs roughly N-squared peerings — with a hub-and-spoke where each network has just one attachment.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has twenty buildings that all need to reach each other. Peering is like building a private bridge between every pair — with twenty buildings that is around a hundred and ninety bridges, impossible to manage. A Transit Gateway is a central transport hub, like a shared metro station: each building builds just one connection to the station, and the station routes people between any two buildings. Add a new building, and it only needs one connection to the station, not a bridge to every other building.

**One line to remember:** Transit Gateway is a central hub that gives transitive routing between many VPCs and on-prem with one attachment each, replacing the unmanageable N-squared mesh of peerings.

sections.s2_technical:
VPC peering is point-to-point and non-transitive, so to fully connect N VPCs you need N times N-minus-one over two peering connections, and traffic cannot flow through an intermediate VPC. For three or four VPCs that is fine; for twenty it is a nightmare of connections and routes, and it cannot include on-premises networks cleanly.

A Transit Gateway solves this by being a hub. Each VPC creates one attachment to the Transit Gateway, and on-premises networks attach through a VPN or Direct Connect. The Transit Gateway then routes between all of them transitively — VPC A can reach VPC C through the gateway even though they are not directly peered. Adding a new VPC means one new attachment and a route update, not a new connection to every existing VPC.

```text
# Each VPC's route table sends inter-VPC traffic to the Transit Gateway
10.0.0.0/16   → local
10.0.0.0/8    → tgw-0hub   (all other bank VPCs reachable via the hub)

# The Transit Gateway's own route table knows every attachment's CIDR
10.1.0.0/16 → attach-prod     10.2.0.0/16 → attach-staging
172.16.0.0/16 → attach-onprem (via VPN)
```

The Transit Gateway has its own route tables, which is what makes it powerful. You associate attachments with a route table and propagate routes into it, and that controls which attachments can see which routes — enabling isolation between environments, which is a separate question. The gateway is regional, scales to thousands of attachments, and supports inter-region peering between Transit Gateways for a global bank network.

A senior nuance: Transit Gateway has a per-attachment and per-gigabyte cost, so for just two or three VPCs that will never grow, plain peering is cheaper and lower-latency. The hub-and-spoke pays off at scale and when you need on-premises connectivity and centralized control. Also, routing through the hub adds a small latency hop compared to direct peering, which for most banking workloads is negligible but worth knowing.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has production, staging, shared-services, and an on-premises data center that all need to communicate. A full mesh of peerings would be unmanageable and cannot cleanly include on-prem. This is exactly what a Transit Gateway hub solves: one attachment each, transitive routing.

Problem 2 — Adding a new VPC must be cheap and not require touching every other VPC. This is exactly the hub-and-spoke advantage: a new spoke adds one attachment.

We will build a `TransitGateway` that registers attachments and routes packets transitively between any two, contrasted with counting the peerings a full mesh would need. Classes: `Attachment`, `TransitGateway`, `MeshComparator`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Transit Gateway with four attachments — production, staging, shared-services, and the on-premises network via VPN.

Step 1 — Each network attaches once to the Transit Gateway. Production announces 10.1.0.0/16, staging 10.2.0.0/16, shared-services 10.3.0.0/16, and on-prem 172.16.0.0/16.

Step 2 — Production sends traffic to 172.16.5.9 in the on-premises data center. The gateway finds that the on-prem attachment owns that range and routes the packet to it transitively — production and on-prem are not directly peered, yet they communicate through the hub.

Step 3 — Staging sends traffic to 10.3.1.1 in shared-services. The gateway routes it to the shared attachment. Any attachment can reach any other through the single hub.

Step 4 — The `MeshComparator` shows the payoff. A full mesh of four VPCs would need six peering connections, and this grows quadratically. With the Transit Gateway it is four attachments, growing linearly. Adding a fifth VPC adds one attachment instead of four new peerings.

```
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] prod → 172.16.5.9: via tgw-0hub → attachment 'onprem' (transitive)
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] staging → 10.3.1.1: via tgw-0hub → attachment 'shared' (transitive)
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Peerings a full mesh of 4 VPCs needs: 6
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Attachments with Transit Gateway:      4
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Mesh (peering, N=4): 6 connections, non-transitive
    prod──staging  prod──shared  prod──onprem
    staging──shared  staging──onprem  shared──onprem

  Hub (Transit Gateway, N=4): 4 attachments, transitive
            ┌──────── tgw-0hub ────────┐
            │          │          │    │
          prod      staging    shared onprem(VPN)
    prod → tgw → onprem  (transitive, no direct link)
```

                    ┌───────────────────┐
                    │  Transit Gateway  │ (regional hub, own route tables)
                    └───┬───┬───┬────┬──┘
          attach │      │   │   │    │ VPN/DX
                 ▼      ▼   ▼   ▼    ▼

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Transitive Routing ═══

  ┌─ Patterns ─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Hub registry: attachments own CIDRs; hub routes by owner │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: TransitGateway routes; MeshComparator counts topology │
  │ O: new attachments added without changing routing logic  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────────┐ * ┌──────────────┐
  │ TransitGateway   │◇─→│ Attachment   │
  │ + attach(a)      │   │ name, cidr   │
  │ + route(from,ip) │   │ + owns(ip)   │
  └──────────────────┘   └──────────────┘
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ MeshComparator   │  meshPeerings = n(n-1)/2, hub = n
  └──────────────────┘

  Contract for route(from, destIp):
    Pre:  attachments registered
    Post: returns the owning attachment (transitive), else no route
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
AWS Transit Gateway is a regional network transit hub that connects many VPCs and on-premises networks through one centrally-managed gateway. Each VPC attaches once, on-premises networks attach through a VPN or Direct Connect, and the gateway provides transitive routing between every attachment. That transitivity is the key difference from peering, because VPC peering is point-to-point and non-transitive, so traffic cannot flow through an intermediate VPC.

The problem it solves is scale. To fully connect N VPCs with peering you need roughly N-squared-over-two connections — for twenty VPCs that is around a hundred and ninety peerings, each with routes to maintain on both sides, and it cannot cleanly include on-premises networks. A Transit Gateway turns that into a hub-and-spoke: each network has a single attachment to the hub, and the hub routes between all of them. Production can reach the on-premises data center through the gateway even though they are not directly peered, and adding a new VPC means one new attachment and a route update rather than a new connection to every existing VPC.

What makes the Transit Gateway especially powerful is that it has its own route tables. By associating attachments with a route table and propagating routes into it, I control exactly which attachments can see which routes, which is how I isolate environments like production from non-production while still allowing the connectivity I want. It is regional, scales to thousands of attachments, and can peer with Transit Gateways in other regions for a global bank network.

At National Bank of India we moved from a tangle of peerings to a Transit Gateway once we had production, staging, shared-services, and the on-premises data center all needing to talk. Each attaches once to the hub, new VPCs join with a single attachment, and the on-prem connection comes in over VPN to the same hub, so everything is centrally managed. The senior point I always add is that this is a scale and control decision, not an always-correct one — for just two or three VPCs that will never grow, plain peering is cheaper and has slightly lower latency, because the Transit Gateway bills per attachment and per gigabyte and adds one routing hop. The hub-and-spoke earns its cost precisely when you have many networks, on-prem connectivity, and a need for centralized, transitive routing.
